{{Short description|Practice of throwing a coin in the air to choose between two alternatives}}
{{Redirect-several|Flipping a Coin (song)|Coin Flip (Shrinking){{!}}Coin Flip {{(-}}''Shrinking'')|Heads and Tails (disambiguation)|Heads or Tails (disambiguation)|dab=off}}
[[File:Coin Toss (3635981474).jpg|thumbnail|Tossing a coin, here a German [[Euro|€1 ]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=German_euro_coins&oldid=1341157101|title=German euro coins|date=March 1, 2026|via=Wikipedia}}</ref>]]
'''Coin flipping''', '''coin tossing''', or '''heads or tails''' involves launching a [[coin]] in the air and then checking [[obverse and reverse|which side is showing]] once it has landed, in order to randomly choose between two alternatives. It is a form of [[sortition]] which inherently has two possible outcomes. Used in such a fashion, the coin serves as a [[binary lot]].

== History and nomenclature ==
[[File:Pompey by Nasidius.jpg|left|thumb|A Roman coin with the head of [[Pompey|Pompey the Great]] on the obverse and a ship on the reverse]]

Coin flipping was known to the Romans as ''navia aut caput'' ("ship or head"), as some coins had a [[ship]] on one side and the head of the [[Roman Emperor|emperor]] on the other.<ref name="Alleyne">{{cite news |last=Allenunne |first=Richard |date=2009-12-31 |title=Coin tossing through the ages |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/science/science-news/6911921/Coin-tossing-through-the-ages.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180210235117/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/science/science-news/6911921/Coin-tossing-through-the-ages.html |archive-date=2018-02-10 |access-date=2012-12-08 |work=[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]}}</ref>
In England, this was referred to as ''cross and pile'',<ref name="Alleyne"/><ref name="bartleby">{{cite web |year=1898 |title=Cross and Pile |url=http://www.bartleby.com/81/4384.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181106191537/https://www.bartleby.com/81/4384.html |archive-date=2018-11-06 |access-date=2012-12-08 |work=Dictionary of Phrase and Fable |publisher=[[Bartleby.com]]}}</ref> "pile" denoted the reverse side, a usage dating back to Medieval times.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.oed.com/dictionary/pile_n2?tab=meaning_and_use|title=pile, n.² meanings, etymology and more &#124; Oxford English Dictionary|website=Oed.com|access-date=June 1, 2026}}</ref> In France the term is inverted: ''pile ou face''. Dutch has ''kop of munt'' (head or coin), Spanish ''cara o cruz'' (face or cross), German ''Kopf oder Zahl'' (head or number), Portuguese ''cara ou coroa'' (face or crown), Polish ''rzut monetą (''coin toss)'','' or (less commonly) ''orzeł czy reszka'' (eagle or remainder, i.e.[[Coins|change]]), and in Czech simply ''hod mincí'' (toss of a coin).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.world-coin-flip.com/|title=Flip a Coin Online in Every Country of the World |website=World-coin-flip.com}}</ref>

==Process==
During a coin toss, the coin is thrown into the air such that it rotates edge-over-edge an unpredictable number of times. Either beforehand or when the coin is in the air, an interested party declares "heads" or "tails", indicating which side of the coin that party is choosing. The other party is assigned the opposite side. Depending on custom, the coin may be caught; caught and inverted; or allowed to land on the ground. When the coin comes to rest, the toss is complete and the party who called correctly or was assigned the upper side is declared the winner.

It is possible for a coin to land on its side, usually by landing up against an object (such as a shoe) or by getting stuck in the ground, and sometimes even on a flat surface. A computational model suggests that the chance of a coin landing on its edge and staying there is about 1 in 6,000 for an American nickel.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Murray|first1=Daniel B.|last2=Teare|first2=Scott W.|date=1993-10-01|title=Probability of a tossed coin landing on edge|url=http://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevE.48.2547|journal=Physical Review E|volume=48|issue=4|pages=2547–2552|doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.48.2547|pmid=9960889|bibcode=1993PhRvE..48.2547M|archive-date=2019-12-15|access-date=2016-03-06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191215073616/https://journals.aps.org/pre/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevE.48.2547|url-status=live|url-access=subscription}}</ref> The thickness of a fair coin, taking into account the coin landing on its third side as a third option, has been the subject of research both experimentally and in statistical mechanics.
The ratio of the thickness of the coin to its diameter is thought to be between 0.577 and 0.866.<ref name="n748">{{cite journal | last1=Hernández-Navarro | first1=Lluís | last2=Piñero | first2=Jordi | title=Exact face-landing probabilities for bouncing objects: Edge probability in the coin toss and the three-sided die problem | journal=Physical Review E | volume=105 | issue=2 | date=17 February 2022 | issn=2470-0045 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.105.L022201 | url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevE.105.L022201 | access-date=15 March 2026 | page=| url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="v105">{{cite journal | last1=Bosso | first1=Pasquale | last2=Huber | first2=Anthony | last3=Todorinov | first3=Vasil | title=Experimental test of fair three-sided coins | journal=European Journal of Physics | volume=42 | issue=2 | date=1 March 2021 | issn=0143-0807 | doi=10.1088/1361-6404/abce1f | page=025802 | url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6404/abce1f | access-date=15 March 2026| url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="v492">{{cite journal | last=Subramanian | first=Gopinath | title=Thickness of a three-sided coin: A molecular dynamics study | journal=Physical Review E | volume=103 | issue=4 | date=26 April 2021 | issn=2470-0045 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.103.L041301 | url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevE.103.L041301 | access-date=15 March 2026 | page=| url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The coin may be any type as long as it has two distinct sides. Larger coins tend to be more popular than smaller ones. Some high-profile coin tosses, such as those in the Cricket World Cup and the Super Bowl, use custom-made ceremonial medallions.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://m.rediff.com/cricket/report/icc-want-to-bid-for-piece-of-world-cup-history-find-out-how/20150322.htm|title=Want to bid for piece of World Cup history? Find out how...|work=[[Rediff.com]]|date=March 22, 2015|access-date=March 30, 2018|archive-date=November 6, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181106180336/https://m.rediff.com/cricket/report/icc-want-to-bid-for-piece-of-world-cup-history-find-out-how/20150322.htm|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://mentalfloss.com/article/29913/brief-history-super-bowl-coin-toss|title=A Brief History of the Super Bowl Coin Toss|publisher=[[Mental Floss]]|last=Allen|first=Scott|date=February 5, 2012|access-date=March 30, 2018|archive-date=December 21, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181221180911/http://mentalfloss.com/article/29913/brief-history-super-bowl-coin-toss|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Three-way===
Three-way coin flips are also possible, by a different process {{Ndash}}too{{clarify|date=August 2026}}, which can be done either to choose one or two out of three. To choose two out of three, three coins are flipped, and if two coins come up the same and one different, the different one loses (is out), leaving two players. To choose one out of three, the previous is either reversed (the odd coin out is the ''winner'') or a regular two-way coin flip between the two remaining players can decide. The three-way flip is 75% likely to work each time it is tried (if all coins are heads or all are tails, each of which occur 1/8 of the time due to the chances being 0.5 by 0.5 by 0.5, the flip is repeated until the results differ), and does not require that "heads" or "tails" be called.
A well-known example of such a three-way coin flip (choose two out of three) is dramatized in ''Friday Night Lights'' (originally a [[Friday Night Lights: A Town, a Team, and a Dream|book]], subsequently [[Friday Night Lights (film)|film]] and [[Friday Night Lights (TV series)|TV series]]), wherein three [[University Interscholastic League|Texas high school]] football teams use a three-way coin flip.<ref name="Bissinger_1990">{{cite book |last=Bissinger |first=H. G. |author-link=H. G. Bissinger |title=Friday Night Lights: A Town, a Team, and a Dream |publisher=Da Capo Press |year=1990 |isbn=9780306809903 |chapter=Chapter 13: Heads or Tails |access-date=2012-12-08 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RWWdLFoFxUYC&pg=PA252}}</ref><ref name="Lee_2008">{{cite news |last=Lee |first=Mike |date=2008-11-07 |title=SAISD athletic director looks back on 1988's famous coin-flip |url=http://www.gosanangelo.com/news/2008/nov/07/saisd-athletic-director-looks-back-on-1988s-coin/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130730114200/http://www.gosanangelo.com/news/2008/nov/07/saisd-athletic-director-looks-back-on-1988s-coin/ |archive-date=2013-07-30 |access-date=2012-12-08 |newspaper=[[San Angelo Standard-Times]]}}</ref> A legacy of that particular 1988 coin flip was to reduce the use of coin flips to break ties in Texas sports, replacing them with [[Tiebreaker#In tournaments and playoffs
|point systems]] to reduce the frequency of ties.

===Larger numbers<span class="anchor" id="HeadsAndTails"></span>===
{{redirect-distinguish|Heads and Tails (crowd game)|Heads and Tails (card game)}}
"Heads and Tails" or "Heads or Tails" is an informal game of chance using repeated coin tosses, suitable for a roomful of seated people, typically a social or children's event. Initially all players stand. Before each coin toss, all still standing put their hands on either their head to indicate "heads" or their hips or buttocks to indicate "tails"; once the toss result is announced, those who guessed incorrectly sit down. The process repeats until the last player standing wins; often the last few players remaining are called to the announcer's table for the climax. A variant with faster elimination is played with two coins and players placing each hand separately.<ref>{{multiref|{{cite web |title=Best Man's Speech |first=Jonathan |last=Rigg |url=https://www.hitched.co.uk/wedding-speeches/best-man-speech-examples/jonathan-rigg_87/ |website=hitched.co.uk |access-date=14 November 2024 |date=1 October 1999 |archive-date=12 December 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241212053845/https://www.hitched.co.uk/wedding-speeches/best-man-speech-examples/jonathan-rigg_87/ |url-status=live }}|{{cite web |last=Foran |first=Amanda |title=Heads or Tails? People are Flipping for this Raffle |url=https://www.readysetauction.com/rsablog/2011/11/14/heads-or-tails-people-are-flipping-for-this-raffle/ |website=ReadySetAuction Blog |access-date=14 November 2024 |date=14 November 2011 |archive-date=21 July 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240721141257/https://www.readysetauction.com/rsablog/2011/11/14/heads-or-tails-people-are-flipping-for-this-raffle/ |url-status=live }}|{{cite web |last=Murad |first=Claire |title=Live Auction Fundraiser Idea-Heads And Tails Game |url=https://muradauctions.com/live-action-fundraiser-idea-heads-and-tails-game/ |website=Murad Auctions |access-date=14 November 2024 |date=7 October 2016 |archive-date=12 December 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241212055625/https://muradauctions.com/live-action-fundraiser-idea-heads-and-tails-game/ |url-status=live }}|{{cite web |last=Parle |first=Rory |title=Heads or Tails |url=https://roryparle.com/2006/10/heads-or-tails/ |access-date=14 November 2024 |date=9 October 2006 |archive-date=12 December 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241212074557/https://roryparle.com/2006/10/heads-or-tails/ |url-status=live }}}}</ref>

==Use in dispute resolution==
[[File:Coin toss at Super Bowl 43 1.jpg|thumb|The coin toss at the start of [[Super Bowl XLIII]]]]

Coin tossing is a simple and unbiased way of settling a dispute or deciding between two or more arbitrary options. In a [[game theory|game theoretic]] analysis it provides even odds to both sides involved, requiring little effort and preventing the dispute from escalating into a struggle. It is used widely in [[sport]]s and other [[game]]s to decide arbitrary factors such as which side of the field a team will play from, or which side will attack or defend initially; these decisions may tend to favor one side, or may be neutral. Factors such as [[wind]] direction, the position of the sun, and other conditions may affect the decision.{{citation needed|date=August 2025}} In team sports it is often the [[captain (sports)|captain]] who makes the call, while the umpire or [[referee]] usually oversees such proceedings. A competitive method may be used instead of a toss in some situations, for example in basketball the [[jump ball]] is employed, while the [[face-off]] plays a similar role in ice hockey.

[[File:1970 Anglo-Italian Cup - Juventus v Sheffield Weds - Coin toss.jpg|thumb|left|Juventus F.C. – Sheffield Wednesday F.C. coin toss]]
Coin flipping is used to decide which end of the field the teams will play to and/or which team gets first use of the ball, or similar questions in football matches, [[American football]] games, [[Australian rules football]], [[volleyball]], and other sports requiring such decisions. In the U.S. a specially minted coin is flipped in [[National Football League]] games; the coin is then sent to the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]], and other coins of the special series minted at the same time are sold to collectors. The original [[XFL (2001)|XFL]], a short-lived American football league, attempted to avoid coin tosses by implementing a [[face-off]] style "opening scramble," in which one player from each team tried to recover a loose football; the team whose player recovered the ball got first choice. Because of the high rate of injury in these events, it has not achieved mainstream popularity in any football league (a modified version was adopted by [[X-League Indoor Football]], in which each player pursued his own ball), and coin tossing remains the method of choice in American football. (The [[XFL (2020–2023)|revived XFL]], which launched in [[2020 XFL season|2020]], removed the coin toss altogether and allowed that decision to be made as part of a team's [[home advantage|home field advantage]].)

In an [[association football]] match, the team winning the coin toss chooses which goal to attack in the first half; the opposing team kicks off for the first half. For the second half, the teams switch ends, and the team that won the coin toss kicks off. Coin tosses are also used to decide which team has the pick of going first or second in a [[penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]]. Before the penalty shoot-out was introduced in the early 1970s, coin tosses were occasionally needed to decide the outcome of drawn matches where a [[Replay (sports)|replay]] was not possible. The most famous instance of this was the semi-final game of the [[UEFA Euro 1968|1968 European Championship]] between [[Italy national football team|Italy]] and the [[Soviet Union national football team|Soviet Union]], which finished 0–0 after extra time. Italy won, and went on to become European champions.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rsssf.org/tables/68e.html|title=European Championship 1968|date=1968|website=[[RSSSF]]|access-date=26 July 2014|archive-date=14 November 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151114222727/http://www.rsssf.com/tables/68e.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[File:BradmanAllenToss.jpg|right|thumb|Tossing a coin is common in many sports, such as [[cricket]], where it is used to decide which team gets the choice of bowling or batting first. Shown are [[Don Bradman]] and [[Gubby Allen]] [[toss (cricket)|tossing for innings]].]]
In [[cricket]] the [[toss (cricket)|toss]] is often significant, as the decision whether to bat or bowl first can greatly influence the outcome of the game. Factors such as pitch conditions, weather and the time of day are considered by the team captain who wins the toss.

Similarly, in [[tennis]] a coin toss is used in professional matches to determine which player serves first. The player who wins the toss decides whether to serve first or return, while the loser of the toss decides which end of the court each player plays on first.

In some other sports, the result of the toss is less important, and is merely a way to choose fairly between two more or less equal options.

[[Fédération Internationale d'Escrime]] rules use a coin toss to determine the winner of some [[fencing]] matches that remain tied at the end of a "[[sudden death (sport)|sudden death]]" extra minute of competition. Although in most international matches this is now done electronically by the scoring apparatus.{{citation needed|date=December 2012}}
===United States sports===
The National Football League also has a coin toss for tie-breaking among teams for playoff berths and seeding, but the rules make the need for coin toss, which is random rather than competitive, very unlikely. A similar procedure breaks ties for the purposes of seeding in the [[NFL draft]]; these coin tosses are more common, since the tie-breaking procedure for the draft is much less elaborate than the one used for playoff seeding.

[[Major League Baseball]] once conducted a series of coin flips as a contingency on the last month of its regular season to determine home teams for any potential [[one-game playoff]] games that might need to be added to the regular season. Most of these cases did not occur. From the [[2009 MLB season|2009 season]], the method to determine home-field advantage was changed.<ref name="MLB_2009">{{cite press release |title=Ownership approves two major rules amendments |date=2009-01-15 |publisher=[[Major League Baseball]] |url=http://mlb.mlb.com/news/press_releases/press_release.jsp?ymd=20090115&content_id=3745318&vkey=pr_mlb&fext=.jsp&c_id=mlb |access-date=2012-12-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090121182633/http://mlb.mlb.com/news/press_releases/press_release.jsp?ymd=20090115&content_id=3745318&vkey=pr_mlb&fext=.jsp&c_id=mlb |archive-date=2009-01-21}}</ref>

In the [[United States]] [[Asa Lovejoy]] and [[Francis W. Pettygrove]], who each owned the claim to the land that would later become [[Portland, Oregon]], wanted to name the new town after their respective hometowns of [[Boston, Massachusetts]] and [[Portland, Maine]]; Pettygrove won with the flip of a coin which has been preserved as the [[Portland Penny]].<ref name = "Orloff">{{cite encyclopedia |last = Orloff |first = Chet |title = Francis Pettygrove (1812–1887) |encyclopedia = The Oregon Encyclopedia |publisher = Portland State University |url = http://www.oregonencyclopedia.org/articles/pettygrove_francis_1812_1887_/ |access-date = March 29, 2010 |archive-date = May 17, 2014 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140517155302/http://www.oregonencyclopedia.org/articles/pettygrove_francis_1812_1887_/ |url-status = live }}</ref>

In addition to its practical applications in sports, coin tossing is symbolic of the democratic principle of equal opportunity. When two parties face an impasse, the act of flipping a coin signifies a commitment to impartiality and a willingness to accept the outcome, no matter how arbitrary it may seem. This shared acceptance of chance as the ultimate arbiter can foster cooperation and conflict resolution in various aspects of life beyond sports, including business negotiations and interpersonal conflicts.

In duels a coin toss was sometimes used to determine which combatant had the sun at his back.<ref name="Scribner_1876">{{cite journal |year=1876 |title=French Duels |url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1876/01/23/84801975.pdf |url-status=live |journal=[[Scribner's Monthly]] |volume=11 |page=546 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210702104212/https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1876/01/23/84801975.pdf |archive-date=2021-07-02 |access-date=2018-06-13}} Reprinted in
{{cite news |date=1876-01-23 |title=French Duels |url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1876/01/23/84801975.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210702104212/https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1876/01/23/84801975.pdf |archive-date=2021-07-02 |access-date=2018-06-13 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref>

==Game==
The party who calls the side that is facing up when the coin lands wins.

The precedent necessity for win in the dual state flip has motivated methods for cheating so as to improve or ensure a win in an apparently random event.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.wikihow.com/Win-a-Coin-Toss|website=wikihow.com|title=How to Win a Coin Toss|date=March 21, 2025 |publisher=[[wikiHow]]|access-date=|via= Gregory P. Harmer, Derek Abbott (1999) www.eleceng.adelaide.edu.au/personal/dabbott/publications/NAT_harmer1999.pdf "biased coins"}}</ref>

==Politics==

===Australia===
In December 2006, Australian television networks [[Seven Network|Seven]] and [[Network Ten|Ten]], which shared the broadcasting of the [[2007 AFL Season]], decided who would broadcast the [[2007 AFL Grand Final|Grand Final]] with the toss of a coin. Network Ten won.<ref name="AFL coin flip">{{cite web|url=https://www.smh.com.au/sport/ten-wins-afl-grand-final-coin-toss-20061222-gdp3ra.html|title=Ten wins AFL grand final coin toss|date=December 22, 2006|access-date=September 22, 2019|publisher=The Sydney Morning Herald|archive-date=September 22, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190922170338/https://www.smh.com.au/sport/ten-wins-afl-grand-final-coin-toss-20061222-gdp3ra.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Canada===
In some jurisdictions, a coin is flipped to decide between two candidates who poll equal number of votes in an [[election]], or two companies [[call for bids|tendering]] equal prices for a project. For example, a coin toss decided a [[Toronto|City of Toronto]] tender in 2003 for painting lines on 1,605&nbsp;km (about 1,000 miles) of city streets: the bids were $161,110.00 ($100.3800623 per km), $146,584.65 ($91.33 per km, exactly), and two equal bids of $111,242.55 ($69.31 per km, exactly).

===Philippines===
"[[Sortition|Drawing of lots]]" is one of the methods to break ties to determine a winner in an election; the coin flip is considered an acceptable variant. Each candidate will be given five chances to flip a coin; the candidate with the most "heads" wins. The 2013 mayoral election in [[San Teodoro, Oriental Mindoro]] was decided on a coin flip, with a winner being proclaimed after the second round when both candidates remained tied in the first round.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://newsinfo.inquirer.net/410339/coin-toss-breaks-tie-in-mayoral-race-in-oriental-mindoro-town |title=Coin toss breaks tie in mayoral race in Oriental Mindoro town |first=Madonna |last=Virola |newspaper=[[Philippine Daily Inquirer]] |date=2013-05-16 |access-date=2013-03-16 |archive-date=2013-05-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130517055041/http://newsinfo.inquirer.net/410339/coin-toss-breaks-tie-in-mayoral-race-in-oriental-mindoro-town |url-status=live }}</ref>

===United Kingdom===
In the United Kingdom, if a local or national election has resulted in a tie where candidates receive exactly the same number of votes, then the winner can be decided either by [[Drawing lots (decision making)|drawing straws/lots]], a coin flip, or drawing a high card from a pack of cards.<ref name="BBC_2000">{{cite news |date=2000-05-05 |title=Hague savours local victories |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/in_depth/uk_politics/2000/local_elections/736660.stm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061028005546/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/in_depth/uk_politics/2000/local_elections/736660.stm |archive-date=2006-10-28 |access-date=2012-12-08 |work=[[BBC News]] |quote=There are two methods to decide the outcome in the event of a draw - either a coin is flipped or the parties draw straws.}}</ref><ref name="BBC_2001">
{{cite news |date=2001-02-17 |title=The count |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/news/vote2001/hi/english/voting_system/newsid_1171000/1171887.stm |access-date=2012-12-08 |work=Vote2001 |publisher=BBC News |quote=He or she ''[the [[returning officer]]]'' can use any random method such as tossing a coin, but the recommended way is to ask each candidate to write their name on a blank slip of paper and place it in a container.}}</ref>

===United States===
In the [[United States]], when a new state is added to the Union, a coin toss determines the [[Classes of United States senators|class of the senators]] (i.e., the election cycle in which the term each of the new state's senators will expire) in the [[US Senate]].<ref name=SenateFAQ>{{cite web |url=https://www.senate.gov/general/common/generic/NewCongress_faq.htm |title=Frequently Asked Questions about a New Congress |publisher=United States Senate |access-date=June 11, 2013}}</ref> Also, a number of states provide for "drawing lots" in the event an election ends in a tie, and this is usually resolved by a coin toss or picking names from a hat.{{citation needed|date=July 2019}} A 2017 election to the 94th District of the [[Virginia House of Delegates]] resulted in a tie between Republican incumbent [[David Yancey]] and Democratic challenger Shelly Simmonds, with exactly 11,608 votes each. Under state law, the election was to be decided by drawing a name from a bowl, although a coin toss would also have been an acceptable option. The chair of the Board of Elections drew the [[film canister]] with Yancey's name, and he was declared the winner.<ref>[https://www.npr.org/2018/01/04/573504079/virginia-republican-david-yancey-wins-tie-breaking-drawing Virginia Republican David Yancey Wins Tiebreaker Drawing] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180104163724/https://www.npr.org/2018/01/04/573504079/virginia-republican-david-yancey-wins-tie-breaking-drawing |date=2018-01-04 }} NPR</ref> Additionally, the outcome of the draw determined control of the entire House, as Republicans won 50 of the other 99 seats and Democrats 49. A Yancey win extended the Republican advantage to 51–49, whereas a Simmonds win would have resulted in a 50–50 tie. As there is no provision for breaking ties in the House as a whole, this would have forced a power sharing agreement between the two parties.<ref>[https://wtop.com/virginia/2017/12/gop-questions-ballot-in-1-vote-margin-va-recount/ Newport News House race tied after judges count outstanding ballot] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171222104947/https://wtop.com/virginia/2017/12/gop-questions-ballot-in-1-vote-margin-va-recount/ |date=2017-12-22 }} WTOP.com</ref>

==Physics==
The outcome of coin flipping has been studied by the mathematician and former magician [[Persi Diaconis]] and his collaborators. They have demonstrated that a mechanical coin flipper which imparts the same initial conditions for every toss has a highly predictable outcome, the [[phase space]] being fairly regular. Furthermore, in flipping by hand people generate a slight bias {{Ndash}}"coin tossing is fair to two decimals but not to three. That is, typical flips show biases such as 0.495 or 0.503."<ref name="persi">{{cite web |url=http://www-stat.stanford.edu/~cgates/PERSI/papers/thinking.pdf |title=The Problem of Thinking Too Much |first=Persi |last=Diaconis |author-link=Persi Diaconis |publisher=Department of Statistics, Stanford University |date=11 December 2002 |access-date=10 April 2009 |archive-date=19 October 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131019160106/http://www-stat.stanford.edu/~cgates/PERSI/papers/thinking.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In studying coin flipping, to observe the rotation speed of coin flips, Diaconis first used a [[strobe light]] and a coin with one side painted black, the other white, so that when the speed of the strobe flash equaled the rotation rate of the coin, it would appear to always show the same side. This proved difficult to use, and rotation rate was more accurately computed by attaching floss to a coin, such that it would wind around the coin {{Ndash}}after a flip, one could count rotations by unwinding the floss, and then compute rotation rate as flips over air time.<ref name="persi"/>

Moreover, their theoretical analysis of the physics of coin tosses predicts a slight bias for a caught coin to be caught the same way up as it was thrown, with a probability of around 0.51,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://news.stanford.edu/news/2004/june9/diaconis-69.html |title=Lifelong debunker takes on arbiter of neutral choices |first=Esther |last=Landhuis |publisher=Stanford Report |date=June 7, 2004 |access-date=February 17, 2012 |archive-date=February 14, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220214230602/https://news.stanford.edu/news/2004/june9/diaconis-69.html |url-status=live }}</ref> though a 2009 attempt to verify this experimentally at Berkeley with 40,000 tosses gave ambiguous results.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/Real-World/coin_tosses.html |title=40,000 coin tosses yield ambiguous evidence for dynamical bias |first=David |last=Aldous |publisher=Department of Statistics, University of California, Berkeley |access-date=2009-10-29 |archive-date=2010-07-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100717220651/http://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/Real-World/coin_tosses.html |url-status=live }}</ref> A much larger 2023 University of Amsterdam study (which won a 2024 [[Ig Nobel Prize]]<ref>{{cite news |last=Hir |first=Vivian |date=September 19, 2024 |title=The Ig Nobel Prize ceremony returns to MIT for the first time in 20 years |url=https://thetech.com/2024/09/19/ig-prize-twenty-four |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241008222802/https://thetech.com/2024/09/19/ig-prize-twenty-four |archive-date=October 8, 2024 |access-date=October 14, 2024}}</ref>) performed 350,757 tosses, finding an average same-side bias of 50.8%, but which varied from person to person.<ref>{{cite news |last=Hooper |first=Ben |date=April 2, 2024 |title=Study indicates coin flips are not exactly 50/50 |url=https://www.upi.com/Odd_News/2024/04/02/netherlands-coin-flip-probability-study/3261712075199/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240425011616/https://www.upi.com/Odd_News/2024/04/02/netherlands-coin-flip-probability-study/3261712075199/ |archive-date=April 25, 2024 |access-date=October 14, 2024 |work=UPI}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/scientists-destroy-illusion-that-coin-toss-flips-are-50-50/ |date=January 1, 2024 |title=Scientists Destroy Illusion That Coin Toss Flips Are 50–50 |last=Shi En Kim |magazine=[[Scientific American]] |archive-date=September 20, 2024 |access-date=October 14, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240920155352/https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/scientists-destroy-illusion-that-coin-toss-flips-are-50-50/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Since the images on the two sides of actual coins are made of raised metal, the toss is likely to slightly favor one face or the other if the coin is allowed to roll on one edge upon landing. Coin spinning is much more likely to be biased than flipping.{{fact|date=October 2024}}

Stage magicians and gamblers, with practice, are able to greatly increase the same-side-up bias, while still making throws which are visually indistinguishable from normal throws.<ref name="persi"/> Conjurers trim the edges of coins so that when spun on a surface, they usually land on a particular face.{{cn|date=October 2023}}

==Counterintuitive properties==
[[File:penney_game_graphs.svg|thumb|upright=1.3|Graphs of best responses for Penney's games of sequence lengths 3 and 4—each sequence is dominated by the sequence pointing to it with the given probability (''italics'') or odds (normal text)<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://researchgate.net/figure/Best-response-strings-for-strings-of-length-3_tbl1_353285025|title=Best response strings for strings of length 3. &#124; Download Scientific Diagram|website=Researchgate.net|access-date=29 March 2023|archive-date=14 February 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230214144928/https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Best-response-strings-for-strings-of-length-3_tbl1_353285025|url-status=live}}</ref>]]
Human intuition about [[Bayes' theorem|conditional probability]] is often very poor (see [[gambler's fallacy]]) and can give rise to some seemingly surprising observations. For example, if the successive tosses of a coin are recorded as a string of "H" and "T", then for any trial of tosses, it is twice as likely that the triplet TTH will occur before THT than after it. It is three times as likely that "THH will precede HHT" than that "THH will follow HHT";<ref>{{cite web |url=http://mathworld.wolfram.com/CoinTossing.html |title=Coin Tossing |publisher=Wolfram MathWorld |access-date=2006-04-02 |archive-date=2009-02-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090215180328/http://mathworld.wolfram.com/CoinTossing.html |url-status=live }}</ref> see also [[Penney's game]].

==Mathematics==
The mathematical abstraction of the statistics of coin flipping is described by means of the [[Bernoulli process]]; a single flip of a coin is a [[Bernoulli trial]]. In the study of statistics, coin-flipping plays the role of being an introductory example of the complexities of statistics. A commonly treated textbook topic is that of [[checking if a coin is fair]].

===Telecommunications===
{{further|Commitment scheme}}
There is no reliable way to use a true coin flip to settle a dispute between two parties if they cannot both see the coin {{Ndash}}for example, over the phone. The flipping party could easily lie about the outcome of the toss. In [[telecommunications]] and [[cryptography]], the following algorithm can be used:

# Alice and Bob each privately choose a random word, e.g. <code>bubblejet</code> and <code>knockback</code>, respectively.
# Alice privately decides to call "tails" on the coin flip.
# Bob sends Alice his chosen word <code>knockback</code>.
# Alice computes a [[cryptographic hash]] of a string that includes the two chosen words and the call (e.g. <code>bubblejet knockback tails</code>), and sends that hash (e.g. <code>3fe97d8e6456a1dce4508d00251345e3</code>) to Bob.
# Bob performs the physical coin flip, and announces the result, heads or tails, to Alice.
# Alice reveals that the string she hashed was <code>bubblejet knockback tails</code>, including both of their words and a call of <code>tails</code>
# Bob confirms for himself that <code>3fe97d8e6456a1dce4508d00251345e3</code> is the hash of <code>bubblejet knockback tails</code>
# Both parties can now determine whether Alice's call of "tails" matched Bob's coin.

Bob, by providing his own random word, guarantees that Alice is not able to precompute an image pair of "tail/random string" or "head/random string", for two different random words. Bob is also unable to reverse Alice's hash to see what her chosen outcome was before flipping the coin, and to lie effectively about its outcome, because he does not know Alice's random word at that point in the process.

==Lotteries==
The [[New Zealand]] [[lottery]] game [[New Zealand Lotteries Commission|Big Wednesday]] uses a coin toss. If a player matches all six of their numbers, the coin toss will decide whether they win a cash jackpot (minimum of NZ$25,000) or a bigger jackpot with luxury prizes (minimum of NZ$2 million cash, plus value of luxury prizes). The coin toss is also used in determining the Second Chance winner's prize.

==Clarification of one's wish==
A technique attributed to [[Sigmund Freud]] to help in making difficult decisions is to toss a coin not actually to determine the decision, but to clarify the decision-maker's feelings. He explained: "I did not say you should follow blindly what the coin tells you. What I want you to do is to note what the coin indicates. Then look into your own reactions. Ask yourself: Am I pleased? Am I disappointed? That will help you to recognize how you really feel about the matter, deep down inside. With that as a basis, you'll then be ready to make up your mind and come to the right decision."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.harveymackay.com/columns/archives/2009-05-28.cfm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110724182534/http://www.harveymackay.com/columns/archives/2009-05-28.cfm |archive-date=24 July 2011 |title=Decision making defines the leader |first=Harvey |last=Mackay |date=28 May 2009}}</ref>

Danish poet [[Piet Hein (Denmark)|Piet Hein]]'s 1966 book ''[[Grook]]s'' includes a poem, "A Psychological Tip", on a similar theme:

{{poem quote|Whenever you're called on to make up your mind,
And you're hampered by not having any,
The best way to solve the dilemma, you'll find,
Is simply by spinning a penny.
No—not so that chance shall decide the affair
While you're passively standing there moping;
But the moment the penny is up in the air,
You suddenly know what you're hoping.}}
